items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: Harry Shields was the last one he knew of that actually harmonized with the trumpet player

ctx.x: Yeah, the Ori band always used it. Of course, Bud Scott, in the days I heard him, he always played guitar, too. He could play banjo, might have done it on a few special numbers sometime, but almost always just guitar. And the Ori band also softened down a lot at times. I mean, they had a lot of variety and dynamics, you might say. But that was part of the old New Orleans tradition, and Jelly talks about it, but Jelly also talks about they would be probably New Orleans bands, too. He was objecting to, being loud.…

Al Rose was telling me that when he grew up listening in the bands that the clarinet and the trumpet always were in harmony together, and the clarinet was not a counterpoint to the trumpet, but he rarely hears that now, that Harry Shields was the last one he knew of that actually harmonized with the trumpet player.

Yeah, occasionally some of the other musicians do it today, but to me, I never heard music here before, say 1930, 38 maybe, it was the first time I ever heard any music here. And so all we have to do, go by, are the old records. But to me, that's been more, to me, a more later development. Some people try to make a big difference between the terms like Dixieland and traditional New Orleans jazz and all, which is mainly just words in people's minds. Because like Bunk once said, we always called it ragtime, and…
